pages:
The entity dissolves.

Not dramatically - it simply stops. The light holding its form redistributes into the chamber walls. The room quiets. After centuries of waiting, it has finished its task.

The Architects were thorough. Whatever they designed this for, they built it to last.

The chamber responds.

Patterns trace themselves in Fracture-light across the stone - not random, not decorative. Language. Architect notation, older than any text in Aetheria's libraries. You recognize it. You shouldn't be able to, but you do.

The Keystone Protocol has been executed. The circuit is complete. The notation reads: acknowledged.

You think about what Elowen said, what the Masked Contact said, what Harla warned you about before you opened the Vault. They were all right about pieces of it. None of them saw the whole design.

The Fracture wasn't a wound. It was a door held open by intention - the Architects left it ajar for exactly this. For someone who could walk both sides of it. For the circuit to close itself through a person, not a machine.

That person was always going to be you. The only question was when.

The hum is gone.

The background resonance you stopped noticing because it never stopped - the deep Fracture-frequency that sat under every quiet moment since Caelmora - has been absent for several minutes before you realize it.

The world is just a world. No pull. No sense of something watching from the deep structure of things. Whatever the Architects sealed into this Protocol has been spent. Completed. Released.

Aetheria is breathing out for the first time in a century.

The path back through the chamber is unchanged. The same stone, the same silence. But the Fracture-marks on the walls are dark now - not threatening, not dormant. Finished.

Elowen will want a debrief. The factions will have questions you can't fully answer. The world will keep moving - councils forming, old alliances fraying, new ones written in the margins of the old ones. You'll be part of that.

But here, in this chamber, with the Protocol complete and the circuit closed:

It's done. You're the last person who will ever need to come here.

That's enough.
ending.title: The Keystone Completes

ALL_DUNGEONS.locked_lore: There are places in Aetheria that remain sealed until the right conditions are met - not by mechanism, but by design. The Architects were precise about this. The path to such a place cannot be found until the circuit that leads there is complete.

ALL_DUNGEONS.name: The Keystone Chamber

boss.lore: It has no face. It has no body in any consistent sense. What it has is a record - of every crossing event, every Fracture activation, every moment a living being of sufficient depth interfaced with Architect substrate. It has been keeping this record for longer than anyone has kept time in Aetheria. It is not hostile. It does not know how to be anything other than what it was made to be. That does not mean it will stop.
boss.name: The Index

phases.desc: It observes before it responds. The first thing the Index does with anything new is measure it.
phases.name: Initialising

phases.desc: It has your combat pattern. Physical contact becomes data it writes against you - every strike feeds the record rather than disrupting it.
phases.immune_hint: Physical contact is redirected into the scar walls - the Index writes the impact into its record and returns it as Fracture-light. Spirit-shaping reaches what blades are only contributing to.
phases.name: Pattern Recognition

phases.desc: It is writing its final entry. You are the subject. The record requires you to hold still. It is not going to wait.
phases.immune_hint: The Index has absorbed your casting signature and is using it as a structural component. Your own spells are part of the record now. Direct physical force is the only thing it has not yet catalogued.
phases.name: Final Compilation

penetrating.land: ENTRY WRITTEN - the record is inscribed straight through your guard.
penetrating.windup: The Index stops writing. Every mark in the chamber turns to face you.

pages:
The Index stops.

Not defeated - completed. Whatever entry it was compiling, it has finished compiling it. The pressure behind its form releases, and the light that held it redistributes into the scar walls the same way breath redistributes into cold air.

The scar does not close.

But the venting slows. Across all seven of the Scholars' mapped fissure points, the instruments register a pressure drop at the same moment - within a single second of each other. Vael will calculate the interval later and find it too precise to be coincidence. She will not say what she thinks that means.

The permafrost floor is warm where the Index stood.

You cannot explain this. You won't be able to, later, when Vael asks - and she will ask, three times, from three different angles, because she is thorough and because the answer matters. Davan will say something sardonic about heat transfer that isn't actually wrong but isn't actually what happened. Osric will write it down without comment and add it to the file that already has your name at the top.

The warmth isn't from the Index. It was always here. The Index was just the first thing that came close enough to show it.

You think about what Vael told you, the first night in Greyfen: that the scars here never hummed. That the south has its hum and the north has its pulse and the two frequencies have never been the same instrument.

When the Keystone Protocol completed, the hum stopped. You felt it stop. The whole south felt it stop. That was real. That was done.

But the pulse is still going.

The Architects built their Protocol on top of something they found here - something already running, already counting, already keeping its record. They used it. They didn't make it. The Protocol closed what the Architects opened. It was never wired to close what was here before them.

Nobody in the south knew to ask.

The Fracture weather above Greyfen that night is different.

The Scholars come out to watch it - all of them, even Osric, who rarely goes outside after dark. The branching patterns in the sky are brighter than anything in their eleven years of observation logs, and they are structured. Not random, not decorative. Something that could be language, if you knew the register.

Vael stands beside you for a long time without speaking. Then she says: 'The hum in the south ended when you closed the circuit. We felt it stop, even here.' A pause. 'Ours never hummed. Ours pulse. Whatever it was you finished - it finished exactly what it was built to finish. This was never part of that design.'

She goes back inside. The patterns continue.

The signal does not dissipate.

You watch it long enough to be sure. It is moving - not spreading outward the way Fracture weather usually spreads, thinning as it goes, but travelling. Structured. Directed.

Southward. Downward through the deep substrate of things, toward the old roots of the world, toward the parts of Aetheria that were old before anyone arrived to name them.

No one sends it back.

Not yet. But something, in the dark below the oldest ground you know, has just been told that the Index has completed its record. And the silence that follows is not the silence of nothing there.

It is the silence of something drawing breath.
ending.title: The Index Completes

Silently, at intervals the Scholars have measured down to the second but cannot explain. Whatever the Architects built their Protocol on top of, the scar predates it. The Scholars know this. They have been careful about how loudly they say it.

adventurer.20: The Adventurer's Hall in Ashford posts contracts that few bother to read. You've read them all.
adventurer.40: Your reputation precedes you across the Mire Road. Highwaymen have begun routing around you.
adventurer.60: The Hidden Court has a name for people who operate at this level without choosing a faction: 'convenient.'
adventurer.80: The Ashford Commons Council keeps your name in a file marked 'asset.' You haven't decided if that's flattering.
adventurer.99: Your name appears in enough reports across enough factions that the Shard Wardens have created a dedicated folder.

aetheric_tending.20: The first harvest comes back richer than the seed cost. Patience is what the plots teach, before anything else.
aetheric_tending.40: You've stopped treating the harvest as the destination. The growth in between has become the work.
aetheric_tending.60: The plots continue without you. The Whisperwood has always worked that way. You have finally learned to match it.
aetheric_tending.80: The rarest crops require conditions only a practiced tender recognises. You have stopped guessing what those conditions are.
aetheric_tending.99: What you grow outlasts any single session of watching it. In the Whisperwood, that is the whole lesson.

alchemy.20: The first tonic is thin and well-intentioned. Every alchemist in Aetheria started exactly where you are.
alchemy.40: The potions carry past the brewing bench now. You have started building your plans around them.
alchemy.60: What you brew bends time in small ways - a window where the body does something it ordinarily cannot.
alchemy.80: The Grove's healers have stopped correcting your method. That is how you know you have one.
alchemy.99: You brew things that change the terms of what is possible. In Aetheria, that is the oldest definition of craft.

attack.20: Accuracy is memory. The body learns what the mind once decided.
attack.40: The Ashford fighting schools teach this level in three years. You compressed it.
attack.60: Experienced fighters read an opponent in the first exchange. You've begun reading them before it starts.
attack.80: The Fracture-touched variants are faster, stranger, less predictable. So are you.
attack.99: Every strike is a decision made before the thought. That is mastery - and, the old fighters say, how the Architects designed combat into Aetheria.

cooking.20: In Aetheria, food is survival first and comfort second. You've mastered the first.
cooking.40: A well-cooked meal in Ashford's rougher quarters is the fastest way to be trusted. You've noticed.
cooking.60: You've started adding things the recipes don't list - instinct the traders call 'ghost flavour.'
cooking.80: The Mire Road camps pay double for your rations. Word travels faster than caravans.
cooking.99: What you prepare now sustains more than hunger. It sustains the will to keep going. In Aetheria, that is not a small thing.

crafting.20: Aetheria's materials are stranger than they look. So is what you do with them.
crafting.40: The Ashford market has started to recognize your work before it's labelled.
crafting.60: Craft at this level means understanding what something wants to become, not just what you need it to be.
crafting.80: The crossed artisans - those who remember other worlds - say your hands work like someone who did this before. Perhaps they're right.
crafting.99: What you make outlasts you. In Aetheria, that is the closest thing to permanence anyone has found.

defence.20: The first blow you don't take is better than the best heal you'll ever eat.
defence.40: Caelmora's knights spend a decade reaching this proficiency. You have the record.
defence.60: You've begun to move before the strike lands - not prediction, something slower and deeper.
defence.80: The Hollow Knights of Caelmora were legends before corruption took them. You exceed their documented peak.
defence.99: The best defence is not a wall. It is understanding the attack well enough that walls become unnecessary.

fishing.20: The rivers near Ashford move slow and cold. What moves beneath them moves slower.
fishing.40: Some catches feel less like luck and more like permission. You've stopped arguing with the distinction.
fishing.60: The spirit-touched fish began appearing in your nets. You didn't ask them to.
fishing.80: Tideward's waters are supposedly impassable for anyone below your level. Supposedly.
fishing.99: You've fished the same water long enough to know its moods. It has started to know yours back.

hp.20: Aetheria punishes the fragile. You are no longer fragile.
hp.40: You've taken enough to know how much more you can take. The number keeps rising.
hp.60: Other fighters notice the moment you stop flinching. Enemies notice it first.
hp.80: The Fracture-touched don't distinguish between tough opponents and impossible ones. You are in their second category.
hp.99: You have survived everything Aetheria has placed in your path. It has run out of arguments.

magic.20: The Architect Spire beneath Ashford still hums. Those with enough Fracture Arts can feel it through stone.
magic.40: Fracture Arts in Aetheria are not learned. They are remembered - something your Earth-self stored without knowing.
magic.60: The Ashen Accord recruits specifically for this level of ability. You've declined that invitation by existing outside their reach.
magic.80: Oraewyn's floating islands were raised by mages at this tier. Three centuries ago. The islands haven't come down.
magic.99: You've reached the level the Architects used as a threshold. Beyond this, their records stop - not for lack of room, but lack of language.

meditation.20: Your mind has learned to go quiet. In Aetheria, that is rarer than ore.
meditation.40: The fragments are not dreams. You've accepted that now. The question is whose memories they are.
meditation.60: You've sat still long enough that Aetheria has begun to sit still with you.
meditation.80: The Order of the Pale Lantern offers Meditation rites at this level. You've already passed where their rites end.
meditation.99: You have gone deep enough to touch the place where Aetheria and memory meet. Whatever is down there knows your face.

mining.20: The ore veins of Caelmora's highlands run deeper than any pickaxe before yours.
mining.40: You've learned to read the rock - where Architect-laced stone has folded into something almost alive.
mining.60: The deeper seams hum faintly. The old surveyors called it resonance. You know better now.
mining.80: The Ashlands await. Drakenhollow's forge clans have a name for someone who mines like you.
mining.99: You do not extract ore. You translate it - raw Aetheria into what it was always becoming.

root_lore.20: The herbs near Caelmora's treeline taste of the forest edge. You have not yet gone deeper.
root_lore.40: The Covenant catalogues what you harvest before you know what you are looking for. That gap is closing.
root_lore.60: You have started reading the deep growth by texture and scent before you know the names. The forest taught you that.
root_lore.80: The Warren's rarest plants grow where no record reaches but yours. You know how to find them.
root_lore.99: You read the Whisperwood from below. The Covenant has a word for someone who gathers like this. They use it carefully.

shadow_arts.20: Not everyone in Aetheria operates in daylight. You've learned why.
shadow_arts.40: The Greyfen exile scholars call it 'peripheral truth' - things that exist only when you stop looking directly at them.
shadow_arts.60: The Ashen Accord's shadow network has noticed your work. They've chosen not to interfere. That is either respect or a trap.
shadow_arts.80: What you practice now has a different name in Greyfen. They use it with reverence.
shadow_arts.99: Shadow is not absence. It is the Architects' first medium - the space between decisions where Aetheria was drafted.

smithing.20: The forge demands patience from everyone. From you, it has begun to demand less.
smithing.40: The Drakenhollow clans have a phrase: sek vorrath - 'the iron remembers.' You're starting to understand it.
smithing.60: What you shape now lasts. The Caelmora armourers noticed first. They haven't stopped watching since.
smithing.80: Forge-masters in Drakenhollow earn their titles after thirty years. You are ahead of schedule.
smithing.99: The metal does not resist you. That is the mark. Everything else was practice.

spirit_harvesting.20: The resonance nodes don't appear for everyone. That they appear for you is not an accident.
spirit_harvesting.40: Shard Dust is what remains when Architect code loses its container. You collect the echoes.
spirit_harvesting.60: The nodes pulse in patterns. You haven't decoded them yet. The word 'yet' is doing a lot of work.
spirit_harvesting.80: You're harvesting what the Fracture left behind. It does not object. You find that more unsettling than resistance would be.
spirit_harvesting.99: You are Fracture-attuned. The resonance nodes light before you arrive. The Architects would recognize what you've become.

spiritbond.20: The companion chose you as much as you chose it. That difference matters more the longer the bond holds.
spiritbond.40: A bonded creature does not follow orders. It negotiates. You have started to hold up your end of the conversation.
spiritbond.60: Your companion forages through hours you cannot see. The bond is what brings it back.
spiritbond.80: The Covenant's oldest guides kept companions for decades. The creature beside you is starting to understand what that means.
spiritbond.99: What you have built is not ownership. The Whisperwood's oldest bond has no word that fits, and that is the point.

spiritweaving.20: The foci you weave hold charge longer than the merchants' stock. Nobody's told you why yet.
spiritweaving.40: Spirit doesn't flow - it chooses. You have learned to be worth choosing.
spiritweaving.60: The Spiritweaving masters of Oraewyn, if you ever reach their floating city, will not be surprised to see you.
spiritweaving.80: What you craft now carries a faint resonance signature. Not crafted. Authored.
spiritweaving.99: The Architects wove reality from spirit. You've learned the first vocabulary of a language they spoke fluently.

strength.20: Aetheria's gravity is not quite Earth's. Your body adapted faster than most.
strength.40: The weight you carry now would have stopped you at the gates of Caelmora.
strength.60: Strength in Aetheria is not purely physical. The spirit-touched know this. Enemies feel it.
strength.80: The mountains between Caelmora and Greyfen are called the Ironbacks. You understand the name differently now.
strength.99: The Architects built Aetheria to be survivable. They did not build it to be easy. You have made it easy.

woodcutting.20: The forests near Caelmora are young by Aetheria's count. The ones further east remember the Architects.
woodcutting.40: Some trees step aside for your axe. That is not metaphor.
woodcutting.60: You've started to hear the pause before a tree falls - a silence that feels like held breath.
woodcutting.80: Whisperwood's ancient groves are said to hold memory in their rings. You're starting to believe it.
woodcutting.99: Every log is a year of the world condensed. You've cut more history than most scholars have read.

changes: Changed: Whisperwood's Nature branch of the skill tree has 12 nodes and 4 expansion auto passives, not the 15 nodes and 5 auto passives listed in the 1.2.0 notes. The tree itself is unchanged. Only the count was wrong.

Fixed: Several screens named Whisperwood content to players who do not own it. The spellbook no longer lists Warren Call or Heartroot Rune. Combat and Shadow Arts food pickers no longer show Whisperwood meals at quantity 0. Item info no longer names Alchemy or Whisperwood sources on base materials. The Hardcore dungeon checklist no longer names Whisperwood dungeons you do not own.

Fixed: Closing the game overnight now credits a potion that was still running at the start of the away window. Previously that overlap was dropped on a cold start, even though the same potion was credited if you only minimised the app.

Fixed: New characters now generate daily and weekly tasks and adventurer contracts immediately, so progress you make before opening those screens is credited. The Standard character-create warning no longer says there are no leaderboards (they shipped in 1.1.2) and no longer claims the character is fully local-only. Cloud save exists.

Fixed: The Achievements button in the Menu now counts only achievements you can actually earn. Without Whisperwood that is 48, not 61. Whisperwood achievements still appear in the count once you own the expansion.
Fixed: The Meditation Memory Archive no longer flashes and rebuilds every few seconds while Auto-Meditate is running. It now only rebuilds when a new fragment actually unlocks.
Improved: Tapping Continue to Game after an offline report now shows Loading before the hitch into the game, instead of looking like the tap was missed.
Improved: Switching to Combat and opening Inventory hitch less. Those panels are kept instead of rebuilt from scratch, and inventory quantities update in place.
Fixed: Quest total-level gates no longer briefly count expansion skills you do not own on load. A non-owner could see a quest as available for a moment, then have it flip back after a refresh.
RELEASES.title: Whisperwood Visibility, Overnight Potion Credit, and Load Hitches

changes: New: Whisperwood, The Living Wilds, is Kaldreth's first expansion. It is a one-time in-app purchase at $5.99 and it opens a living forest west of the known map, with two sub-zones: The Canopy above the treeline and The Root Warren beneath the soil. Inside: 20 new quests, raising the quest total from 66 to 86; 15 new monsters, raising the Bestiary roster from 72 to 87; 69 new items, raising item collection from 529 to 598; 14 new Shadow Arts targets, raising the total from 107 to 121; 13 new achievements, raising the total from 48 to 61; a new title, Rootkeeper, for finishing the 20 quest arc; and a new faction, the Grove Covenant, with 4 reputation tiers. Everything named below as Whisperwood content sits behind that purchase. If you do not buy it, the game you have today is unchanged: no base game bar moves, nothing you have already earned is touched, and no existing content becomes harder to complete.

New: Four new skills come with Whisperwood. Root Lore is a gathering skill with 9 nodes, and it unlocks from the first Whisperwood quest. Aetheric Tending grows 8 crops on plots. Alchemy brews 16 recipes, split across tabs. Spiritbond binds companions. All four sit alongside the 16 base game skills rather than replacing anything in them.

New: Aetheric Tending plots and Root Lore foraging run on the wall clock rather than your action slot. A plot takes between 30 minutes and 16 hours to come in depending on the crop, and it grows while your character trains something else - planting never interrupts what you are already doing, and foraging works the same way. Because both are deadlines rather than rates, the 4 hour offline cap does not apply to them. A plot planted before bed is ready when you come back, however long that is.

New: Alchemy potions burn wall clock time too, and they do not pause when the app is closed. This is the same model the Fracture Surge already uses. A 20 minute potion drunk just before you shut the game is spent by the time you open it again. Being direct about it: drink them when you are about to play, not on your way out.

New: Seven companions can be bonded through Spiritbond, from the Pale Hound at level 1 up to the Heartwood Elder at level 105. The bond, and which companion is currently at your side, is managed from a new Spiritbond panel.

Changed: Owning Whisperwood raises the skill level cap from 99 to 105 on every skill, including all 16 base game ones. So that base game skills have somewhere to climb into, a new Heartwood rung has been added to each of the 8 existing gathering and artisan ladders, and Spiritweaving gains a new spell, Warren Call, at level 102. An existing maxed character is safe. Skill XP you have already earned is never rewritten, and the cap only governs what the level reads. If the entitlement ever lapses, your levels read 99 again and not one point of XP is lost - buying back restores the level immediately.

New: Two equipment slots have been added, hands and companion, appended to the existing ten. The hands slot closes a long standing gap: gloves items existed in the data but resolved to no slot at all, so there was never any way to wear them. They can be equipped now.

New: Two boss dungeons, The Hollow Root and The Grove's Warden, bring the total from 5 to 7. Each has its own first clear key item and its own memory fragment, matching all five base game dungeons, and both pay into the same Chronicler currency the existing dungeons do.

New: Whisperwood also adds a Nature branch to the skill tree with 15 nodes, 5 new auto passives, and 4 new rows in the Skill Mastery store. Two new kinds of adventurer contract, tending and foraging, run against a deadline rather than occupying your action slot, so they progress while you train something else. An arrival cinematic plays the first time you reach Whisperwood, and there is a hidden meditation vision at level 105.

Changed: Every base game achievement stays fully earnable without buying anything, and buying Whisperwood never raises a base game bar. Two achievements needed repairing to hold that line. "All 99s" and "Jack of All Trades" had already broken when the four new skills entered the data: both counted 20 skills instead of 16, which made them unearnable for every player in the game, buyer or not. Both are now frozen to the 16 base game skills and are earnable again. The same freeze covers the Bestiary completion achievement, the all dungeons clear achievement, and Affinity Mastery, whose description already promised "every base game action". The achievements page now groups into two collapsible tiers, Base Game and Whisperwood, with the existing categories inside each. Whisperwood has its own completionist achievement scored over its own set; it does not feed the base game one.

Fixed: The Greyfen Shadow Arts ladder was inverted end to end. This is a buff to content that shipped in 1.1.0 and it applies to every player, expansion or not. The level 60 entry target, the Outer Watchman, paid 31,937 XP per hour, while the level 95 capstone, the Scar Prefect, paid 26,106. The decline was monotonic across the whole region, so thirty five levels of progression bought strictly less XP per hour than the target you walked in on. The cause was the band multiplier falling away through the mid game faster than the written XP values climbed. Twelve XP values have been raised and nothing has been lowered. Being honest about the size of it: the per rung raises go up to +40%, but no player's best available rate rises by more than about 5%, because every large raise landed on a rung that was already paying below the level 60 entry. Those rungs stop being traps rather than becoming rewards. The light track now runs from 17,885 up to 19,596 and the heavy track from 31,937 up to 33,555, both ascending the whole way. Two pre-existing oddities are deliberately untouched and are not claimed as fixed here: the 2.4x jump on entering Greyfen at level 60, and the light track paying less than the heavy track at the same level.
RELEASES.title: Whisperwood, Four New Skills, and the Level 105 Cap

changes: Fixed: The Warden Permafrost Blade has been corrected. As shipped, it carried attack 16 and strength 12. The resonite blade sits at attack 46 and strength 26, requires three fewer Attack levels to wield, and costs roughly 44,000 gold - the Permafrost Blade required Attack 88 and cost 185,000 gold and was, by every damage metric, a strict downgrade from the tier below it. No damage reduction, XP bonus, or mastery stat offset that. Buying it made your character weaker. It is now attack 58 and strength 33, one tier-step above resonite on the weapon ladder. The blade carries no damage reduction; that is a separate, deliberate earlier decision that stands unchanged. Players who already own it receive the corrected stats automatically on load, with no action needed.

Changed: All items that can be purchased from any vendor are now capped at 100% of their actual purchase price when sold. Previously this cap covered only mastery relics and Greyfen provision items. The path that cap now newly closes is Adventurer vendor gear, which is bought repeatedly with Pathfinder Seals. With a high stack of sell-price bonuses - from faction reputation, fortune skill-tree nodes, and equippable passives - that gear could be sold for more gold than it cost to buy. Pathfinder Seals become a gold source through that loop, and that loop is now closed. Being direct about it: if you were cycling Adventurer vendor gear through your inventory at a sell-price profit, that income is gone. The scope is narrow. Greyfen provisions remain capped at the price you actually pay with any active discount, not the list price. Mastery relics are unchanged. Every item with no vendor purchase path at all is not capped and its sell price is completely unchanged - this correction applies only to gear bought from the Adventurer vendor.
RELEASES.title: Warden Permafrost Blade Correction and Adventurer Vendor Sell Cap

changes: New: Eighteen leaderboards are now available through a new Leaderboards entry in the Menu. Nine cover Standard play, nine cover Hardcore: total level, lifetime gold earned, total kills, kills of The Unwritten, and a clear count for each of the five boss dungeons - Hollow Sanctum, Spire Depths, Accord Vault, Keystone Chamber, and the Fracture Scar. The Leaderboards entry only appears on devices that have Play Games installed. Reaching it requires a signed-in Play Games account, which the game obtains through the cloud-save connect flow on the character select screen - tapping the entry before connecting brings up a prompt explaining how to do that. Boards rank your Google account, not any individual character slot. Play Games keeps the best score ever posted for your account, so a player with several characters is ranked by the strongest one. Standard and Hardcore have entirely separate board sets. A hardcore character that reverts to Standard after a death posts to the Standard boards from that point on - its hardcore entries stand. No reward of any kind is attached to rank. One limitation for existing saves, stated plainly: per-dungeon clear counts were not recorded before this update, only an aggregate total. Any dungeon a character had already cleared before updating starts at a count of one on the leaderboards, regardless of how many times it was actually run. Counting is accurate from this update forward. The aggregate clear total that dungeon achievements read is unchanged.

Fixed: Three quests in the Frostmere arc - Cartography of Damage, Eleven Years of Silence, and the arc's final quest - previously deducted 8, 10, and 15 Accord Remnants reputation respectively. The intent was a narrative cost for siding with the Greyfen Scholars. In practice, Accord Remnants reputation has no recovery path, so completing the arc permanently left a character below full standing with no route back. The reputation penalties are removed. Existing characters who completed those quests and are sitting below where they should be have their Accord Remnants standing corrected automatically on their next load, with no action needed. Greyfen Scholars reputation from those quests is unchanged.
RELEASES.title: Play Games Leaderboards and Accord Remnants Reputation Fix

changes: New: Standard characters can now see how much gold they will lose before confirming a respawn. The amount appears on the death modal and in the Combat and Shadow Arts status text for as long as you are dead. The figure is the exact sum that will be deducted - it already accounts for any respawn gold-loss-reduction bonuses you have, and it respects the existing minimum and maximum caps on the loss. Nothing about how much gold is lost has changed - the deduction, the bonuses that reduce it, and the caps are all the same as before. The only difference is that you can see the number before you commit. Hardcore characters cannot respawn and are unaffected.

New: Dying to The Unwritten now seals the Combat panel for 15 minutes. The Unwritten is the optional super-elite in Frostmere - it is not required for any quest or achievement, but it hits for up to 600 and is built to kill a character in full endgame gear. When you fall to it, the Combat panel is replaced by a fractured display showing what was done to you and a countdown of the remaining seal time. Everything else stays open during that window: gathering, artisan skills, Shadow Arts, quests, and all five boss dungeons are unaffected. If you die to The Unwritten while offline, the lockout counts down against your offline time, so a death early in a long away period has already expired by the time you read the offline report. Respawn is reachable from the sealed panel itself, so the seal never leaves you stuck behind it.
RELEASES.title: Projected Gold Loss on Death and Unwritten Combat Lockout

changes: New: Frostmere, The Shattered Tundra, is a new region in the frozen north beyond the Ironback Mountains. It is home to the Greyfen Scholars, an exiled faction who have spent eleven years mapping the deepest Fracture scars. Reaching it opens a new six-quest line, bringing the quest total to 66. Inside: 41 new monsters, raising the roster from 31 to 72; 60 new items, raising the total from 317 to 377; 14 new Shadow Arts targets, raising the total from 93 to 107; 4 new gathering nodes; 12 new recipes; 5 new achievements, raising the total from 43 to 48; and 3 new titles, raising the total from 12 to 15.

New: The Fracture Scar is the fifth boss dungeon and the hardest content in the game. Entry requires Attack 85, Defence 75, all four existing dungeons cleared, and the quest "Into the Scar". The dungeon boss, The Index, has three phases. The final phase - Final Compilation - uses defence-penetrating attacks that bypass your defence stat entirely. Only gear-based damage reduction and the Scar-Ward Draught reduce hits from that phase. Death inside the Fracture Scar forfeits all loot from that run.

New: Two new gear sets are available in Frostmere and the Fracture Scar. The Warden Permafrost set is ten pieces - armour slots carry defence, accessories carry damage reduction. The Chronicler now sells a Permafrost Aegis upgrade for the Warden mantle, bought with a currency earned inside the Fracture Scar. The Unwritten set is four pieces, dropped only by The Unwritten - an optional super-elite that hits for up to 600 and will kill a character in full endgame gear. It is not required for any quest or achievement.

New: Two new consumables are available alongside the Fracture Scar content. The Scar-Ward Draught grants a 30% reduction to all damage taken for 20 minutes. It is the only item that reduces the defence-penetrating hits from Final Compilation. The Index Echo arms a single killing-blow negation - the next hit that would kill you instead leaves you at 1 HP and ends the fight. You must arm it deliberately from the Inventory before a fight; it does not trigger automatically, and it does not work inside boss dungeons. Both items can be used anywhere in the game.

New: The Bestiary is a new record of every monster in the game, accessible from the Menu. Each entry fills in the first time you kill that monster, showing its stats, drop table with chances, and a lore note. Entries you have not unlocked appear locked. There are 72 entries covering the full monster roster, including the 41 added with Frostmere.

Changed: Sixty new items and 72 new Bestiary entries enter their respective completion trackers this update, and both completion figures will read lower for existing characters the moment they update. The item collection shift is smaller: 60 new items enter the denominator at zero found, so anyone who had reached 100% item collection falls below that. No achievement or title is tied to that number, so nothing already earned is lost - there are 60 new things to find. The Compendium drop is larger. The Bestiary adds 72 entries at zero found for every existing character, shifting the Compendium total from 1,083 to 1,155 entries, so anyone sitting at 100% Compendium completion will drop to around 94% after updating. All 72 are reachable by playing. One Compendium row moves in the other direction: the Affinity Mastery row previously counted 10 Fracture Arts gathering nodes that have no affinity system and could never progress past level 1, capping the row at 206 out of 216 for every character in the game. Completing the row was not possible, even though the achievement behind it was already earnable. Those 10 nodes are no longer counted. Every existing character's Affinity Mastery row can now reach 100%.

New: The monster selection dropdown in Combat has been replaced by a full monster picker. Each monster entry shows a portrait, an archetype badge, a defence bar, a recommended combat style, and your current contract progress where a matching contract is active. A survival readout now sits beside the fight setup: before you start, it calculates whether the selected monster's worst-case hit can kill you at your current HP and shows you the result.

Improved: The setup and run screens for all five boss dungeons have been rebuilt. The setup screen lays out entry requirements and your gear readout more clearly before you commit to a run. The run screen presents phase information and the action row more legibly during a fight. The rebuild was built around the Fracture Scar but applies to all five dungeons, including the four that already existed.

New: Twelve quest NPC portraits have been added across the game - named characters who previously appeared as text only now have faces in dialogue screens. An arrival cinematic plays the first time you reach Frostmere. The Fracture Scar has its own music track and new ambient sound throughout.

Fixed: The title "The Settlement" is now awarded for completing the q60 quest line. That arc is the longest in the game and previously granted no title for finishing it. Existing characters who have already completed it receive the title automatically on load, with no action needed.

Fixed: A boss dungeon achievement check ran before the clear it was testing for had been saved, so a first-time clear could fail to tick its achievement until the following run. All five dungeons were affected. The check now runs after the clear is recorded.

Fixed: Two nodes in the Conquest branch of the skill tree, Trial Ready and Iron Dominance, each promise a mastery point on every boss dungeon clear. The bonus was only applying on the first clear of each dungeon. A player who bought both collected at most 10 mastery points from them across all five dungeons, then nothing more, no matter how many times the dungeons were replayed. Both nodes now pay on every clear. A player holding both earns 2 mastery points per dungeon run from this point on. Past re-runs cannot be credited - the game records whether a dungeon has been cleared, not how many times, so there is nothing to reconstruct. The first-clear nodes in the same branch, First Blood Bonus and Conqueror's Mark, were always correct and are unchanged. The run log also used to label the per-clear mastery point gain as a first-clear reward on every run. It now names the two rewards separately, so a repeat clear says it is a per-clear bonus rather than claiming to be a first clear.

Fixed: Characters created before mastery point totals were written to disk have their total rebuilt on every load by re-counting every source: quest rewards, achievements, auto passives, and the skill tree spend against them. Boss dungeon clears were not included in that count, leaving any such character short the mastery points those clears awarded. Dungeon mastery points are granted once per dungeon, and the game records which dungeons have been cleared, so the missing amount can be calculated exactly. Affected characters receive the correct total on their next load with no action needed. Characters created more recently store the total directly and were never affected.
RELEASES.title: Frostmere, the Fracture Scar, and the Bestiary

changes: Fixed: Six nodes in the Fracture Arts skill tree promised a Fracture Arts affinity XP bonus that never functioned. Fracture Arts has no affinity system, so the stat those nodes referenced does not exist. Players who spent mastery points on them received nothing from that line, and nothing in the game indicated anything was wrong. Three of them had no working effect of any kind: Sigil Adept, Sigil Harmony, and Crystal Attunement. They now grant +8%, +10%, and +8% Fracture Arts XP respectively. The other three, Crystalline Flow, Spire Echo, and Fracture Ascendant, already granted real Fracture Arts XP alongside the non-functional affinity line. Their XP values are unchanged and the dead line has been removed from their descriptions. Anyone who has already purchased any of these six nodes gets the corrected bonus automatically on load, with no action required.

Fixed: Deaths in Shadow Arts and inside boss dungeon runs now count toward your lifetime death total and toward the "The Unrelenting" achievement, which requires falling in battle 200 times. Previously only deaths in overworld combat were recorded. Dying while pickpocketing or mid-dungeon left your count untouched, so a player who never trained in overworld combat could not make progress on the achievement regardless of how many times they fell. All three contexts now count equally. The game also now keeps a per-source and per-killer breakdown of your deaths for potential future use. The UI does not yet surface that breakdown, but the records are being built from this point forward. Existing characters keep the death total they already have, and the new breakdown starts empty for everyone, since there was no way to reconstruct where older deaths happened.

Changed: The Error State phase of the Spire Depths boss now hits harder and applies a deeper defence reduction. Before this update, the Spire Depths was the second dungeon in the sequence with higher entry requirements than the Hollow Sanctum, but the Error State phase was no more dangerous than the Hollow Sanctum boss. Players who had just cleared the first dungeon stepped into the second and found the hardest phase barely more threatening. The Error State now sits where a second-dungeon boss phase should: above Hollow Sanctum and below the Accord Vault. Being direct: if you have already cleared the Spire Depths, it is now harder than it was when you did. Boss health, phase triggers, style immunities, and dungeon rewards are unchanged.
RELEASES.title: Fracture Arts Node Fix, Death Tracking, and Spire Depths Difficulty

changes: Changed: The spelstone cost for the four bar tiers that require it has been halved. Spelcast Bar drops from 2 spelstone to 1, Mirestone Bar from 4 to 2, Fracture Cast Bar from 6 to 3, and Resonite Bar from 8 to 4. These four are the only bar recipes in smithing that call for two separate gathered materials rather than one. The cost also scaled disproportionately at higher tiers: a complete resonite gear set previously needed over 600 spelstone alongside the primary ore. Primary ore cost, craft times, and XP per action are unchanged. Prompted by the Discord community.
RELEASES.title: Spelstone Cost Reduction

changes: Changed: Each combat and Shadow Arts tick can now consume at most two servings of food, regardless of how many healing sources are involved. Previously auto-eat had no limit per tick - it would eat through as many servings as it took to keep you alive, so survival scaled with how large your food stack was rather than how much each serving actually healed. The cap is a budget on the tick, not on any single source: auto-eat, the manual Eat button in live combat, and the Eat button inside boss dungeon runs all draw from the same two-serving allowance per tick. Tapping the manual Eat button could previously out-eat what auto-eat was held to; the boss dungeon Eat button had no per-tick limit at all. Both now follow the same rule. The top-up that happens when you start an activity is not a tick and is not capped. Shadow Arts ticks run on the steal cooldown, which is longer than a combat tick, so the two-serving limit means the same practical rate in both places. What this means for you: a character who was staying alive by eating through a large stack of weaker food fast enough will now die in situations where it previously did not. Food quality matters more than food quantity from this point on, and carrying a bigger stack is no longer a substitute for better food or stronger gear. This applies to standard and hardcore characters alike. One note on existing saves: away time banked before this update replays under the old uncapped rules, so nobody comes back to a death decided by a rule that did not exist when they closed the game. Prompted by the Discord community.

Changed: All eight worldroot fusion relics have been raised. Each one costs 20 to 30 tier jewels plus a stack of endgame bars to forge - and before this update every one of them handed back worse returns than the amulets and rings used to make it. They now lead the game on every effect they carry. Skill XP bonuses on all eight go to 22 percent, above both the 12 percent on the inputs and the previous game-wide ceiling of 20 percent. Each relic also gained on its specific stats: the Voidweave Pendant and Shadowveil Crown now carry the highest stealth in the game; the Voidweave Pendant's shadow-arts bonus item chance now leads the game; the Mastercraft Signet's artisan cycle reduction now beats the tier rings that forge it; the Ironblood Torc's HP regen interval reduction now leads the game. Two exceptions, stated plainly: combat damage and combat defence on the Ironblood Torc and Warden's Ascendant Band go up, but stop at the top of the jewellery category rather than matching dungeon weapons and mantles. Damage percent is the strongest stat in the game, and both relics sit in slots that stack with each other - pushing them to dungeon-weapon level would have roughly doubled player damage. The Shadowveil Crown's spirit harvesting yield bonus is also deliberately unchanged: it is a flat addition that gets multiplied by other bonuses afterward, and raising it would have tripled the architect-shard economy. Prompted by the Discord community.

Changed: The crafted woodwork off-hand line has been rebuilt. The top of the line was giving worse defence than mid-game generated gear - the level 90 Architect's Aegis sat at 14 defence while a generated buckler from level 45 content could reach 26. Defence values now track what a same-tier generated buckler provides: the Pale Willow Ward rises from 7 to 9, the Ashwood Bulwark stays at 11, and the Architect's Aegis rises from 14 to 22. Craft times and XP per action across the line have been reset so that XP per hour rises consistently from the lowest recipe to the highest, and every entry is at least as good as the best crafting XP per hour available elsewhere at that level. Being direct about the downside: the Pale Willow Ward and Ashwood Bulwark now grant less XP per craft than before - 32 down to 25, and 45 down to 21 respectively - and each takes a second or two longer. The Architect's Aegis grants more, rising from 100 to 111. Prompted by the Discord community.

New: Two craftable off-hands fill the gaps in the woodwork line at levels 60 and 75. The Deeproot Rampart (crafting level 60, five Deeproot Logs, 14 defence) and the Vantwood Redoubt (crafting level 75, five Vantwood Logs, 18 defence) are available from the Woodwork crafting tab.

New: A session gains drawer replaces the floating loot feed. The floating labels that drifted over the left side of the screen - showing XP gains, item pickups, and gold earned - are gone. They sat on top of interface text too often and covered content on whichever panel was open. The footer is now a single foldable unit: a handle, a gains row, status chips, and the tab bar together. The gains row keeps running totals for the session as small tokens that flash when they tick up - XP by skill, levels gained, gold, your top items, and an XP per hour readout. Nothing scrolls past and nothing overlaps other content. Tapping the handle folds the gains row and chip strip away together and returns that space to the screen. The fold state is remembered between sessions. Folded, the handle still shows your current activity, the headline totals, and a marker for any pending claims, so collapsing never hides work waiting to be picked up. Offline gains replay through it the same way live play does.

Improved: Combat and Shadow Arts each now fit on one screen without scrolling. In Combat, your level and stat tiles fold behind a Details control, and the area, monster, food, auto-eat, spell, and style selectors fold behind a Fight Setup header that shows a summary of what is hidden. The enemy portrait moves to the background of the enemy card, dimmed behind the content, so the loot grid sits over the artwork rather than below it. Loot lists in both tabs are now two columns of chips with the drop chance under each name, and they expand to fill whatever height the collapsed cards leave rather than a fixed fraction of the screen. Shadow Arts gets the same layout for its Setup card. What is expanded and what is collapsed is remembered between tab switches and sessions.

Improved: Every scrollable list in the game now has inertia scrolling. Releasing a drag mid-flick carries the gesture's speed into the list, which glides and decelerates to a stop. Pausing before you lift your finger, or stopping mid-drag, leaves the list exactly where you put it. Touching a gliding list catches it - and that touch does not also activate whatever was under your finger.
RELEASES.title: Auto-Eat Cap, Relic Buffs, and Off-Hand Crafting

changes: Changed: The XP numbers shown everywhere in the game are now ten times larger than they were. A Cairn Rock grants roughly 12 XP where it granted about 1, and level thresholds grew by the same factor. This is a presentation change, not a balance one: at the old scale the slowest early actions were worth less than a full XP point, so the counter appeared not to move through several actions in a row and a gathered resource could show no gain at all. Larger numbers give every action a visible, honest value. The number of actions required to reach any level is exactly the same as before, and existing characters were converted automatically on load - every level and every fraction of progress carries over exactly, nobody was promoted or demoted. All of this is separate from the rate change, which is the main point of this update and is a genuine nerf: every skill's XP gain rate has been cut. Before this, a skill could go from level 1 to 40 inside a single 4-6 hour idle session, and a full 1-99 grind measured around 74 hours of continuous play. That is not an idle-game curve - the whole progression was roughly 10x too fast, and long-term goals did not feel like long-term goals. Now every skill lands around 30 days of continuous idling to reach 99. The early game is deliberately quick - levels 1 to 10 take under an hour for almost every skill - but the mid and late game are where the slower pace is felt, and levels 1 to 40 now take around 10 to 14 hours depending on the skill. Being direct about what this means for you: your skills will level noticeably slower than they did yesterday, offline and overnight sessions will return far fewer levels, and there is no way to soften that. The cut is not one flat number - it varies by skill and by the tier of content you are training on. The level requirement of the node, recipe, or shadow arts target you have selected determines the rate, and higher-tier content still pays better than what it replaces. Unlocking a new tier never leaves you worse off than staying on the one below it. Meditation, Adventurer, and combat skills - Attack, Strength, Defence, and Hitpoints - have no content tier to choose between, so those scale on your own level in that skill instead. Quest XP rewards have been scaled to match. Left unchanged, fixed quest rewards would have handed out something close to Meditation 66 and Attack 60 for free against the new rate. Adventurer contract and vendor XP rewards are scaled in both the reward preview and the actual payout, so the number shown is the number granted. Two flat XP top-ups are scaled to keep their intended weight: the Shard Gleaning affinity bonus at affinity 25 and 50, and the Dockmaster's Hookknife fishing bonus. Left unscaled, each would have been worth more than the full action it was topping up. Both now add a share of a catch or harvest rather than a flat couple of points, which keeps them at the same proportional weight they were always meant to carry.

New: Boss dungeons now have a proper health bar docked directly above the action row, next to the Eat button. Previously your HP was a small text label up in the run header while the button that answers low health sat at the bottom of the screen - tracking your health during a run meant watching two places at once. The bar shows exact HP centred on the fill, a damage trail that briefly holds your pre-hit level before draining down, and quarter markers along the frame. It flashes on hit and on heal. The fill colour and condition wording shift at 60 percent and 30 percent health, the same thresholds the screen's edge vignette already used, and the frame pulses in time with them. The bar carries the warning itself; you do not need to watch anything else.

Fixed: When auto pickpocket was running, the result of each steal attempt was never displayed. A failed steal that damaged or stunned you produced no message at all, so it looked like nothing had happened to your health. On top of that, the damage figure was being recorded before auto-eat ran, so on the occasions something did surface it quoted a health value that did not match what the bars showed. Each resolved steal attempt now reports its outcome - the damage taken, any stun, and the auto-eat line - and the health number quoted matches what you actually see.

Changed: The cost of buying inventory slots has gone up. The base cost per slot rises from 500 to 1250 gold, and the per-slot growth rate increases from 1.04 to 1.045. In practice every expansion now costs at least double what it did, and large expansions scale harder than they used to. Slots already purchased are unaffected - this changes only the price of expansions bought from now on. At the old prices, inventory space stopped being a meaningful decision very early. With the slower XP curve, gold accumulates over a much longer horizon, and how you spend it should be a real choice throughout that time.
RELEASES.title: Skill XP Rebalance, Boss Health Bar, and Inventory Prices

changes: Fixed: On the per-skill Gear screens added in 1.0.10, you could set the same item in both the weapon slot and the off-hand slot of a single skill even when you only owned one copy of it. One copy cannot fill two slots. That second slot also never granted a second bonus - an item's stat contribution counts once per skill no matter how many slots name it - so the duplicate entry only ever looked like it was doing something. The gear picker now shows such an item greyed out with a short note explaining why, instead of letting you assign it. If you own two copies of an item, both slots can still name it - only the case where one copy is already claimed by another slot in the same skill is blocked. Existing characters are repaired automatically on load: where one copy was listed in both slots, the weapon slot keeps it and the off-hand entry is cleared. Nothing was lost - that off-hand entry was never contributing a bonus. Two related display improvements accompany this: a slot whose item is already counted by another slot in the same skill now says so, and a slot that names an item another slot in the same skill has already claimed your only copy of is flagged the same way an unowned item is already shown.

Changed: Boss damage per tick has been reduced by 20 percent across every phase for all four named bosses - the Second Knight in the Hollow Sanctum, the Echo of the Architect in the Spire, the Sealed Accord in the Accord Vault, and the Keystone Entity in the Keystone Chamber. Trash waves leading up to each boss are not affected. Two updates back to back each made correct fixes, and their combined effect was boss fights that are harder than the encounters were built for. In 1.0.9 the combat damage bonus was corrected from being applied twice per hit in boss dungeons - players with heavy skill-tree investment were landing up to roughly 38 percent less damage on bosses afterward, which was the right outcome since the old behaviour was a bug. In 1.0.10 Fracture Arts spell power was compressed and MAG gear values were reduced. Both of those remain as shipped. What they added up to: fights ran longer while bosses hit at the same rate as always, so players were absorbing far more total damage per clear than intended. Reducing boss hit damage by 20 percent restores roughly the pre-1.0.9 total damage taken per run for a player with moderate skill-tree investment. Heavily invested players will still find bosses somewhat harder than they were before 1.0.9 - the double-apply bug helped them most, so absorbing a bit more than the old baseline is appropriate. Boss health, phase mechanics, style immunities, and dungeon rewards are unchanged.

Fixed: Passive HP regeneration now works everywhere and in every state. There were four separate problems, and all four are resolved. First, regeneration only ever started if you stopped a combat session cleanly. Health lost to Shadow Arts, or to a fight that ended any other way - running out of food, for instance - never regenerated at all, so you could walk around indefinitely at low health while fishing, mining, or crafting and the bar would never tick up. Regeneration now starts from any damage from any source, and keeps running whatever you are doing. Second, every 'HP regen interval -N seconds' bonus was doing nothing while the game was open. That covers the Iron Body and Fortification skill-tree nodes, the Pilgrim's Heart mastery, and every piece of gear that lists the stat - the regeneration clock was hardcoded to 12 seconds regardless of what your character sheet said. Those reductions now genuinely apply, down to a floor of one point of health every 2 seconds. The character sheet's 'Regen interval' line was always telling you the truth about what you had earned - the game just was not honouring it. Third, regeneration now continues during combat, during Shadow Arts, and inside boss dungeon runs, instead of stopping the moment you started doing something. This is a genuine buff to survivability in all three, not only a fix - if you have invested in regen nodes or gear, you will notice it. Fourth, regeneration now also catches up while you are away - offline combat and Shadow Arts sessions heal between fights and steals exactly as they would have if you had been watching, rather than the full rest period arriving at once when you open the game. The Warlord's Bundle doubling of regeneration below 30 percent health applies in all of these places too.

Fixed: Level-up celebration cards could log an error when two cards fired in rapid succession and the confetti from the first card had already faded before the second arrived to clean it up. Switching characters while a card was still fading in could trigger the same kind of error. Neither case was likely to crash the game outright, but both are now guarded correctly.
RELEASES.title: HP Regen Overhaul, Boss Damage, and Gear Fixes

changes: Fixed: Equipping the Ashvein Blade locked your combat style to Strength with no way to change it, and the Cairn Blade did the same for Attack. Both are early-game weapons left over from a time when they were the only two blades in the game, and the style restriction was never removed when the weapon roster expanded. Every other blade already allowed any style. Both now offer Balanced, Attack, Strength, and Defence. Staves and wands still restrict to Fracture Arts only - that is intentional, since they carry no melee stats. Reported by the Discord community.

New: Locked Wealth achievements now show a progress bar with your lifetime gold earned from gameplay against the target amount. Previously there was no way to see that running total without unlocking the achievement.

New: The Combat tab now shows kill counts without requiring you to start a fight. Select any enemy and you will see your count for that specific enemy alongside your lifetime total. One caveat worth stating plainly: per-enemy counts begin at zero for existing characters. The game was not tracking kills by enemy type before this update, so there is no older data to carry over. Your lifetime kill total is unaffected - it has always been recorded and carries over correctly.

Fixed: Some Shadow Arts loot showed one drop chance in the Shadow Arts panel and a different, roughly ten times higher rate in the inventory and item info popups. The Shadow Arts panel was the accurate one. Rare equippable pickpocket drops are capped at roughly 0.9 percent, and every screen now shows the same effective rate, including any bonuses from your own gear. Reported by the Discord community.

Fixed: Scrolling inside a popup - affinity bonuses, the item info card, skill explainers, or the spellbook - also scrolled the page behind it. Popups no longer pass scroll input through to the screen underneath them. The same fix addressed a related issue where the content lists inside those popups, and the patch notes list, were difficult to drag-scroll on a phone and often took several attempts. All of them now respond cleanly on the first drag. Reported by the Discord community.

Improved: The Shadow Arts setup dropdowns are now locked and dimmed while auto pickpocket is running, matching the behaviour already in place for the Combat tab during a fight. They can no longer open accidentally while you are scrolling. Prompted by the Discord community.

Changed: Fracture Arts has been brought back in line with melee. At maximum levels and best-in-slot gear, spells were killing roughly three and a half times faster than a maxed melee character. That was not close to intended, and it came from three things stacking that were each reasonable on their own. First, MAG sits on all ten equipment slots with no tradeoff, while metal armour grants no strength whatsoever - only defence - so a fully geared caster carried 144 MAG against a fully geared warrior's 75 strength, and MAG drives both spell damage and spell accuracy, so that gap counted twice. Second, the per-spell power multiplier added in 1.0.9 climbed to more than double on top of that. Third, spell damage rolled a minimum of one third of its maximum where melee rolls from 1, so spells averaged two thirds of their top hit while melee averaged half. Three changes address it together: the spell power curve has been compressed so the strongest spell now sits about 28 percent above Pale Flicker rather than more than double it, MAG values on magic gear have been reduced, and the spell damage minimum is now one quarter of maximum instead of one third. Maxed Fracture Arts still kills about 1.3 times faster than maxed melee, which the sigil cost of every cast earns. Being direct about what this means for you: if you play magic, your character now does less damage than it did yesterday, and there is no way to soften that. Overnight and offline combat is where you will notice it most - a magic character at top gear will come back to roughly 60 percent fewer kills from a full offline window than before. Your magic gear will also read lower MAG on its tooltips than you remember; the items were not swapped or downgraded, the numbers behind every piece were reduced. The gear reduction is weighted toward the top: Pale cloth, the first tier, is completely untouched, and the cuts grow with each tier so that Architect cloth and the Level 99 relics take the largest reduction. Every tier is still a strict upgrade over the one below it. Pale Flicker is unchanged, exactly as it was in 1.0.9. Sigil costs have not changed, so the cheaper spells remain the efficient choice for long grinding sessions and the expensive ones still buy faster kills. Mid-game casters around level 50 keep a comfortable lead over melee at the same point. Melee has not been buffed - nothing about attack, strength, or melee gear changed in this update. The 1.0.9 notes said the top-tier spells would hit roughly twice as hard per cast as Pale Flicker. They did, and that is the part being walked back here. Spell tiers still matter and higher spells still hit harder and land more reliably, just across a much narrower band than we shipped last time.

Changed: Non-combat skills each have their own Gear button now, sitting in the panel header next to Affinity and the ? button - covering mining, woodcutting, fishing, spirit harvesting, smithing, cooking, spiritweaving, crafting, shadow arts, meditation, and adventurer. A skill's bonuses now come solely from that skill's own gear list. Gear worn in a combat preset contributes nothing to a skill, and gear listed under a skill gives no combat stats - each screen shows the full picture for what it controls. If you were keeping skill gear in a combat preset to carry its bonus into training, that no longer works: list those items under the relevant skill's Gear screen instead. The change removes the need to re-equip a shared preset every time you switch which skill you are training. The gear slots work as references, not reservations: listing an item does not move it out of your inventory, and the same item can be listed by any number of skills at once. One Prospector's Lens can serve mining, smithing, and cooking simultaneously - you do not need duplicates. If you sell the last copy of a listed item, the slot stays set and shows 'Not owned' until you acquire another, at which point the bonus applies again. Your existing setup was migrated automatically: gear from the old gathering preset was copied into every non-combat skill's list, and the items were returned to your inventory. If your inventory was full before this update, it may now be over capacity - sell some things before trying to pick up new item types. Combat skills are unaffected: attack, strength, defence, hitpoints, and Fracture Arts still use the three combat presets. The Equipment screen now shows three presets.
RELEASES.title: Fracture Arts Rebalance, Kill Counts, and Per-Skill Gear

changes: Improved: Owners of the Warden's Mark now have all three boosts permanently active - no button presses needed. Auto-Meditate runs continuously, Fracture Surge keeps 2x speed at all times, and the +4h offline cap extension is always in effect. The offline progress cap still applies to Auto-Meditate, so a long absence credits only up to the capped window, the same as before. Non-owners are unaffected - rewarded ad boosts work exactly as they always have.

New: Daily and Weekly task cards now have a 'Go' button on each incomplete task, the same as adventurer guild contracts already had. Tapping it takes you straight to where the task is completed - the relevant skill panel for gathering, crafting, meditation, pickpocketing, and guild-contract tasks; the Combat tab for kill tasks; the Boss Dungeons screen for dungeon tasks; and the Skills list for weekly tasks that cover any skill. Completed tasks show the Claim button as before.

Changed: Fracture Arts spells now each hit for their own damage. Previously, the game applied the same damage formula to every spell regardless of which you cast - your Fracture Arts level and your MAG gear determined the number, and the spell choice changed only the sigil cost. That meant a three-sigil cast did no more per cast than a one-sigil Pale Flicker, making the higher spells a worse trade by any measure. Each spell now has its own strength behind it. Higher-tier spells hit harder and land more reliably than lower ones. Pale Flicker is unchanged - it was the old baseline, so no one comes out weaker. The trade between spells is deliberate: the strongest options deal the most damage per cast but spend the most sigils to do it, so Pale Flicker and the other cheaper spells remain the efficient choice for long grinding sessions. Spending up buys faster kills, not free damage. At high Fracture Arts levels, the top-tier spells hit roughly twice as hard per cast as Pale Flicker.

New: A small 'i' button now sits beside the Spell dropdown in Combat. Tapping it opens the spellbook - a side-by-side listing of every Fracture Arts spell, including ones you haven't unlocked yet. For each spell the panel shows its damage range, its hit chance against the monster you currently have selected, its element, its sigil cost, how much damage it deals per sigil spent, how many casts your current stock affords, and how long that stock would last across a fight. Locked spells display with the Fracture Arts level required to use them, and the relevant quest where one applies. The Spell dropdown itself now shows a short summary of the selected spell's damage and hit chance underneath it, so you can see the key numbers at a glance without opening the full panel. The point of both additions is the same: you can see exactly what you stand to gain before committing sigils.

Fixed: If a skill levelled up quickly - training Fracture Arts early is the easiest way to hit it - celebration cards queued up while your skills panel already showed the real level, leaving a gap of 10 or more that took minutes to clear. Pending levels now merge into a single card showing your current level, the card on screen ends early when more are waiting, and leftover firework particles from an interrupted card no longer drift into the next one.

Fixed: In boss dungeons, your combat damage bonus was being applied twice on every hit - once directly and once again compounded on the result, so the bonus was multiplying against itself rather than applying as a straight addition. Overworld combat was not affected. The result was that players with meaningful investment in the damage skill tree were landing far more damage on bosses than the listed bonus would suggest. The bonus now applies once per hit, which is how it already worked everywhere else in the game. Players with little or no combat damage investment will notice almost no difference. Players who have invested heavily will see boss damage drop by up to roughly 38 percent - the more nodes you carry, the larger the practical reduction. Boss dungeon rewards and boss health are unchanged.
RELEASES.title: Permanent Boosts for Warden's Mark Owners

changes: Changed: Fracture Arts now burns sigils rather than raw materials directly. If you were casting before this update, your spells will fall back to wand melee until you have sigils woven - and you need the Spiritweaving level required for the sigil your spell uses. Check each spell's description for which sigil it takes and weave a stock before your next fight. Six new Spiritweaving recipes cover the spells that needed them: Pale, Ash, Fracture, Stone, Spire, and Resonance Sigils, joining the four that already existed. One gleaned material weaves into five sigils - everything you have stockpiled is still usable, it just needs one extra step first. Lower spells cost one sigil per cast; the strongest cost two or three.

Changed: Sigil sell prices have been reduced. Sigils are now produced five at a time and serve as casting ammunition - the old prices were set when sigils were rare single-output items, and no longer reflect what they are.

New: Every skill now explains what it does. Tapping Attack, Strength, Defence, Hitpoints, or Fracture Arts in the Skills list used to show only 'Trained through combat only' - it now opens a card describing the skill and what each level gives you. Every skill panel also has a '?' button for the same card, and gathering and artisan panels show a one-line description at the top. This covers the skills players had the hardest time reading - Wardcraft, Shard Gleaning, and Spiritweaving in particular. Prompted by the Discord community.
Improved: When you run out of sigils mid-fight, the combat log now names exactly which sigils you are short of and tells you to weave more - previously it reported only that you were out of reagents.
RELEASES.title: Fracture Arts Overhaul, Skill Explainers, and Combat Log

changes: More ad fixes, brought to light by the Discord community.
RELEASES.title: Ad Fixes

changes: Community Event: Post the word Ren in the Kaldreth Discord general chat - the first 5 to do so will receive a promo code for a free Warden's Mark. If you already own it, you were one of the game's earliest supporters and we want to thank you - if and when the first expansion is released, yours is on us.

New: Every skill detail page now shows a level-progress bar with your current XP and the XP needed for the next level. It appears consistently across all skills - Gathering, Smithing, Crafting, Cooking, Meditation, and the rest. Suggested by the Discord community.

Improved: Combat and Shadow Arts now remember your setup when you switch tabs and return. Your chosen monster, area, food type, auto-eat threshold, and attack style are all restored exactly as you left them - previously leaving either tab reset everything to defaults. The Discord community raised this.
Fixed: Improved the reliability of rewarded ad boosts. Reported by the Discord community.

Fixed: On narrow phones, the button rows in Combat and Shadow Arts - configuration, stop, and action controls - stayed side by side when the screen was too small to fit them cleanly, leaving them cramped or running off the edge. They now stack vertically on smaller screens so every control is reachable on any phone size.
RELEASES.title: Skill XP Meter, Persistent Setup, and Ad Reliability

changes: New: A short note from the developer now appears on the character select screen. New players see it directly after the "Welcome to Aetheria" intro; returning players who already dismissed that intro see it on its own. It explains that Kaldreth is a solo project, that the Report a Bug button in Settings is open to any feedback - suggestions, things to add or cut or rebalance, not only bugs - and that Play Store reviews are read.
New: A Community section has been added to Settings with a Join the Discord button. Kaldreth now has a Discord server.
RELEASES.title: Developer Note and Discord Community

changes: Fixed: The ad-gated boosts were not initialising, so Auto-Meditate (4 hours), Fracture Surge (2 hours), and the Extended Offline Cap (+4 hours) all showed "Ad cannot be loaded - unlock with Warden's Mark" for every player. Ads now initialise correctly and all three boosts are accessible.

New: Four story titles are now earnable and visible on the Titles screen: Shard Warden, First Warden, Crown of Fractures, and Fracture's End. Each is granted on completing its respective quest. If you have already finished those quests, the titles are awarded automatically on first load.
Fixed: Crashes that could occur on opening the Skills, Boss Dungeon, Shadow Arts, Titles, Map, and Item Collection screens on certain devices. All six screens now open correctly.
Fixed: Signing out of cloud sync now stays signed out across launches - it was silently re-signing in on the next start.

Fixed: Auto-Meditate sessions simulated during offline progress are now correctly capped to your offline window and can grant the occasional bonus Mastery Point, matching live meditation. The offline report now notes when gathering stopped because your inventory filled up.
Fixed: The Pathfinders faction's offline gathering bonus now applies to offline progress only, as its description states. It was previously also accelerating live gathering.

Fixed: The Ashvein armour set and Mirestone Blade now sell for prices appropriate to their tier - both were priced below lower-tier gear. Contract achievement ranks corrected so "Legendary Adventurer" (1,000 contracts) is the highest tier rather than a mid-tier rank.
Fixed: Quest completion text now correctly names the rewards - two quests were displaying the wrong items in their reward descriptions.
Fixed: The notifications toggle in Settings now saves correctly across launches. It was re-enabling itself on every restart.
RELEASES.title: Rewarded Ad Boosts, Story Titles, and Stability Fixes

changes: New: Combat and Shadow Arts loot panels now show the gold range per kill or pickpocket - for example '12-24 gold' - as a guaranteed top row. The range reflects your current gold bonuses from gear, skill tree, and popularity unlocks. Previously the combat panel showed no gold at all, and the Shadow Arts panel showed only a vague 'Small coin purse' row.

New: 15 items that previously showed a placeholder glyph now have proper icons, including the three Worldroot relics (Verdant Worldcharm, Arcweave Confluence, Bulwark Heartstone), the Shadowveil Crown, five belt and quest items (Dockyard Enforcer Badge, Mirepath Spool, Lantern Initiate Cape, Apothecary Satchel, Dock Scrip), three faction sigils (Noble House Seal, Pale Lantern Seal, Sealed Accord Fragment), and three crafted staves (Deeproot, Emberbark, Vantwood). Three existing icons - Tidebind Rod, Architect Clothwork Leggings, and Vial Bandolier - have been redrawn to better match their items.
RELEASES.title: Gold Loot Ranges, Item Art, and Naming Fixes

changes: New: Affinity XP is now a flat amount granted per action rather than a percentage of skill XP. The progression curve is redesigned: early affinity levels come quickly, later levels require more XP but the ratio from first to last is roughly 7x - not the thousand-fold gap of skill levels. Skills with a large number of affinities (Smithing, Crafting, Shadow Arts) receive proportionally higher XP per action so the total grind scales with breadth, not depth. Magic no longer has an affinity system. Existing affinity data is reset once on first load - old values were incompatible with the new formula, and few players had progressed beyond level 1-5 under it.

Fixed: The death screen details - killer name, fatal hit, HP before the hit, and food info - could render one character per line on some devices, making the panel unreadable. The layout now uses a stacked label structure and displays correctly at all screen sizes.
RELEASES.title: Affinity System Redesign

changes: New: The character select screen now briefly lists the four expansions planned for Kaldreth.

New: Ten achievements added: Annihilator (50,000 enemies defeated), Master Thief (1,000 steals), Tycoon (1,000,000,000 gold earned), Well Rounded (total level 500), Polymath (total level 1,000), Grandmaster (total level 1,500), Dungeon Master (100 dungeon runs), Inner Calm (first meditation), Ascetic (500 meditations), and The Unrelenting (hidden). A Meditation category has been added to the Achievements screen.

New: A death screen now appears when you die in live combat or shadow arts. It shows what killed you, the damage of the fatal hit, your HP before that hit, your auto-eat threshold and food type, and how much food you had left. Standard characters see a Respawn button; hardcore characters see an Acknowledge button that leads into the demotion or retirement choice.

Improved: The offline cap-boost card in the Store can now be refreshed before it expires. Tap the card again and watch another ad to extend the window. Previously it could only be activated once per window.
